units.title: Finding Nouns, Verbs, and Subjects
units.recap: Find the verb first, then ask who or what performed it. A subject sits before an “of” phrase, never inside it. Infinitives (to file) are never the main verb; gerunds (filing) are verbs acting as nouns. Commands have an understood subject: you.

items.prompt: Tap the subject.
items.explanation: Find the verb — surprised — then ask who or what surprised. The verdict did. “Jury's” is a possessive modifier, not the subject.

items.prompt: Tap the subject.
items.explanation: A subject comes before a phrase beginning with “of.” The subject is list (singular), not exhibits — which is why the verb is “was.”

items.prompt: Tap the subject.
items.explanation: Inverted sentence: the verb “were” comes first, so ask what was attached. Declarations — plural, hence “were.”

items.prompt: Tap the main verb (not the helping verbs).
items.explanation: “Had been deliberating” is a three-word verb: had and been are helping verbs; deliberating is the main verb.

items.prompt: In “The court agreed to hear the appeal,” what is “to hear”?
options: An infinitive — not the main verb
items.explanation: A verb preceded by “to” is an infinitive and never the main verb. The main verb here is “agreed.”

items.prompt: In “Filing the brief took three hours,” what job is “Filing” doing?
options: It's a gerund — a verb form acting as the subject
items.explanation: Add -ing to a verb and use it as a noun and you have a gerund (a “verbal noun”). Here it is the subject of “took.”

items.prompt: What is the subject of “Please file the response by Friday”?
options: You — the understood subject of a command
items.explanation: Every request or command has the understood subject you: (You) please file the response.

items.prompt: Tap the subject.
items.explanation: Verb first: emerges. What emerges? A pattern. “Record” is inside a prepositional phrase and can never be the subject.

items.prompt: How many subjects and verbs are in “The clerk drafted the memo, and the judge revised it”?
items.explanation: Clerk drafted / judge revised — two independent clauses, each with its own subject and verb. That is why the comma before “and” is required.

items.prompt: Correct the error — or submit with nothing flagged if the sentence is already right.

errors.explanation: The subject is bundle, not affidavits — the “of” phrase can't contain the subject. Bundle was delivered.

items.prompt: Correct the error — or submit with nothing flagged if the sentence is already right.
Which sentence has a compound subject?
options: The clerk and the intern reviewed the docket.
The clerk reviewed and annotated the docket.
The clerk reviewed the docket and the transcript.
items.explanation: Two nouns doing the verb = compound subject. The second has one subject and two verbs; the third has one subject, one verb, and two objects.

units.title: Subject–Verb Agreement
units.recap: The subject sits before any “of” phrase. Or/either-or/neither-nor: the verb matches the nearer subject. “Along with,” “as well as,” and parentheses never pluralize a subject. With here/there the subject follows the verb. Distances, periods, and sums taken as a unit are singular. Portion words (a lot, some, all, a majority, percent) follow the noun after “of.” Use “were” for wishes and contrary-to-fact statements.

items.prompt: Correct the error — or submit with nothing flagged if the sentence is already right.

errors.explanation: Subject = stack (singular). The “of” phrase never holds the subject.

items.prompt: Correct the error — or submit with nothing flagged if the sentence is already right.

errors.explanation: With neither/nor the verb agrees with the nearer subject — transcript, singular. Reverse the order and “support” becomes correct.

items.prompt: Choose the correct verb: “The witness, along with both attorneys, ____ present.”
items.explanation: “Along with,” “as well as,” “besides,” and “not” are not part of the subject. Ignore them: the witness was present.

items.prompt: Choose the correct opening: “____ several grounds for reversal.”
items.explanation: In here/there sentences the true subject follows the verb. Grounds is plural, so “there are.” Never pair “there's” with a plural.

items.prompt: Choose the correct verb: “Two-thirds of the record ____ been designated.”
items.explanation: Portion words (a lot, some, all, a majority, percent, fractions) take their number from the noun after “of.” Record is singular → has.

items.prompt: Choose the correct verb: “Two-thirds of the exhibits ____ been designated.”
items.explanation: Same rule, opposite result: exhibits is plural, so the portion word takes a plural verb. This is the one place where the “of” phrase does control.

items.prompt: Choose the correct verb: “Five years ____ the maximum sentence for that offense.”
items.explanation: Distances, periods of time, and sums of money take a singular verb when considered as a single unit — five years is one sentence length.

items.prompt: Correct the error — or submit with nothing flagged if the sentence is already right.

errors.explanation: Contrary-to-fact and hypothetical statements take the subjunctive “were,” even with a singular subject: if the statute were ambiguous.

items.prompt: Which is correct?
options: The court ordered that the witness appear on Monday.
The court ordered that the witness appears on Monday.
items.explanation: Demands, requests, and orders take the subjunctive: the base form “appear,” not “appears.” It sounds odd until you notice it everywhere in orders.

items.prompt: Correct the error — or submit with nothing flagged if the sentence is already right.

errors.explanation: Whatever number you give a collective noun, keep it. “Is … they” switches mid-sentence. Either “the panel is … it wants” or recast as “the panel members are … they want.”

items.prompt: Choose the correct verb: “Every exhibit and every declaration ____ been logged.”
items.explanation: “Every X and every Y” distributes over each noun separately and stays singular, even though “and” normally builds a plural.

items.prompt: Correct the error — or submit with nothing flagged if the sentence is already right.
Choose the correct verb: “Either the clerk or the interns ____ the exhibits.”
items.explanation: Either/or: the verb follows the nearer subject — interns, plural. Proximity, not the first noun, decides.

units.title: Irregular Verbs
units.recap: Irregular verbs form the past tense and the past participle unpredictably. The participle is the form that follows a helping verb (has/have/had). Never attach a helping verb to a simple past form — “I have broke” and “had went” are the classic errors. And the simple past can't work as an adjective: a broken dish, never a broke dish.

items.prompt: Choose the correct form: “The panel had already ____ the case when the motion arrived.”
items.explanation: After a helping verb (had) you need the past participle: begun. “Began” is the simple past — it stands alone: the panel began.

items.prompt: Choose the correct form: “Counsel has ____ three extensions this year.”
items.explanation: Seek → sought → sought. Both the past tense and the participle are “sought.”

items.prompt: Correct the error — or submit with nothing flagged if the sentence is already right.

errors.explanation: Go is the oddest irregular: past tense “went,” participle “gone.” After “had” you need the participle — had gone.

items.prompt: Choose the correct form: “The court has ____ this issue twice before.”
items.explanation: Take → took → taken. “Has took” is the error to watch for; after a helping verb it must be taken.

items.prompt: Choose the correct form: “The jury had ____ the verdict form before the recess.”
items.explanation: See → saw → seen. “Had saw” is never right; “seen” cannot stand alone as a past tense either (“she seen it” is substandard).

items.prompt: Correct the error — or submit with nothing flagged if the sentence is already right.
Choose the correct form: “The state ____ the prisoner in 1897.”
items.explanation: When hang means execution by rope, the past is hanged — active or passive. Inanimate objects are hung: the portrait was hung.

items.prompt: Choose the correct form: “The clerk has ____ the corrected order to the parties.”
items.explanation: Send → sent → sent. Straightforward, but it belongs in the drill because it pairs with irregulars that don't behave (like go and take).

items.prompt: Correct the error — or submit with nothing flagged if the sentence is already right.

errors.explanation: Write → wrote → written. After the helping verbs “should have,” the participle written is required.

items.prompt: Which is standard English?
options: The order that was struck contained a typo.
The order that was strucken contained a typo.
The order that was strike contained a typo.
items.explanation: Strike → struck → struck (the archaic “stricken” survives mainly in fixed legal phrases like “stricken from the record”).

units.title: Pronouns
units.recap: Subject pronouns (I, he, she, we, they) do the verb and also rename the subject after “to be.” Object pronouns (me, him, her, us, them) receive action or follow prepositions. After than or as, finish the sentence mentally. Possessive pronouns (its, yours, hers, theirs, whose) never take apostrophes. Use a -self pronoun only when the subject and object are the same person.

items.prompt: Correct the error — or submit with nothing flagged if the sentence is already right.

errors.explanation: Remove “Marisol and”: assigned the opinion to I? No. Objects of prepositions take the object pronoun — to Marisol and me.

items.prompt: Correct the error — or submit with nothing flagged if the sentence is already right.

errors.explanation: Strip the “and” phrase: Her split the memos? No — She split them. Subjects take subject pronouns.

items.prompt: Choose the correct pronoun: “The senior clerk drafts faster than ____.”
items.explanation: Finish the sentence mentally: faster than I draft. The comparison calls for a subject pronoun. (In casual speech “than me” is common; formal writing keeps “than I.”)

items.prompt: “The judge would rather consult her than ____ .” Which pronoun keeps the meaning “rather than consult me”?
items.explanation: Both are grammatical but they mean different things: “than me” = rather than consult me; “than I” = rather than I would consult her. Choose by meaning.

items.prompt: Correct the error — or submit with nothing flagged if the sentence is already right.

errors.explanation: Never use “myself” unless I or me already appears in the sentence. This is a plain object: send it to Judge Alvarez or me.

items.prompt: Which uses the reflexive correctly?
options: The witness and himself reviewed the transcript.
items.explanation: Reflexives work when the subject and object are the same person. They cannot serve as a plain subject or object — that's the puffed-up “myself” error in a different costume.

items.prompt: Correct the error — or submit with nothing flagged if the sentence is already right.

errors.explanation: Possessive pronouns — its, yours, hers, ours, theirs, whose — never take an apostrophe. “It's” is only ever “it is” or “it has.”

items.prompt: Correct the error — or submit with nothing flagged if the sentence is already right.

errors.explanation: Whose = possessive. Who's = who is / who has. Same pattern as its / it's.

items.prompt: Formally correct: “It is ____ who must decide the question.”
items.explanation: Pronouns that rename the subject after a “to be” verb take the subject form: It is we who must decide. (Casual English tolerates “It's us,” but not in an opinion.)

items.prompt: Choose the verb: “It is I who ____ responsible for the delay.”
items.explanation: When “who” refers to a personal pronoun, it takes that pronoun's verb: I am → It is I who am responsible.

items.prompt: Correct the error — or submit with nothing flagged if the sentence is already right.

errors.explanation: “Between” is a preposition, and prepositions take object pronouns: between you and me. “Between you and I” is the most famous hypercorrection in English.

items.prompt: Which sentence keeps its pronouns consistent?
options: Each juror returned to his or her seat. (or: The jurors returned to their seats.)
Each juror returned to their seat, and they were polled.
Each juror returned to his seat, and they were polled.
items.explanation: Singular antecedent, singular pronoun — or rewrite in the plural, which the Blue Book recommends as the cleaner fix. (The 12th edition does accept singular “they” where rewriting isn't practical, but never mixed with a singular pronoun in the same breath.)

units.title: Who, Whom, Whoever, Whomever
units.recap: The they/them test: if “they” fits, use who/whoever; if “them” fits, use whom/whomever. Decide inside the pronoun's own clause and ignore what the rest of the sentence is doing. Beware the pseudo-sophisticated “whom” in constructions like “a judge whom I think is fair” — put “I think” at the end and the error appears.

items.prompt: Choose the correct word: “____ did the panel assign the opinion to?”
items.explanation: Assign it to them → whom. (Formal drafting would recast: “To whom did the panel assign the opinion?”)

items.prompt: Choose the correct word: “We know ____ drafted the dissent.”
items.explanation: Look only at the second clause: they drafted the dissent → who. What the first clause (“we know”) is doing does not matter.

items.prompt: Correct the error — or submit with nothing flagged if the sentence is already right.

errors.explanation: Move “I think” to the end: a jurist whom will be confirmed, I think — obviously wrong. The pronoun is the subject of “will be confirmed,” so who.

items.prompt: Choose the correct word: “Give the assignment to ____ asks for it first.”
items.explanation: They ask for it first → whoever. The whole clause is the object of “to”; inside the clause the pronoun is the subject.

items.prompt: Choose the correct word: “We will hire ____ the committee recommends.”
items.explanation: The committee recommends them → whomever. Here the pronoun is the object inside its own clause.

items.prompt: Choose the correct word: “____ is selected will serve a four-year term.”
items.explanation: They are selected → whoever. The clause “whoever is selected” is itself the subject of “will serve.”

items.prompt: Correct the error — or submit with nothing flagged if the sentence is already right.

errors.explanation: They prevail → whoever. The preposition “to” takes the whole clause as its object, not the pronoun alone — a favorite trap.

items.prompt: Choose the correct word: “The clerk ____ the judge trusts most reviewed the draft.”
items.explanation: The judge trusts them → whom. Strip the sentence to its bones and the case becomes obvious.

items.prompt: Correct the error — or submit with nothing flagged if the sentence is already right.

errors.explanation: The pronoun is the subject of “is calling” — they are calling — so who. “Should I say” is an interposed aside.

items.prompt: Which is correct?
items.explanation: Directly after a preposition, use whom. This one is a fixed formula worth memorizing.

units.title: Who, That, Which
units.recap: Who (and sometimes that) refers to people; that and which refer to groups and things. That introduces an essential clause — information the sentence needs — with no commas. Which introduces a nonessential clause, always fenced by commas. The commas carry meaning: they tell the reader the information could be lifted out.

items.prompt: Correct the error — or submit with nothing flagged if the sentence is already right.

errors.explanation: The clause identifies which provision — essential — so “that,” with no commas.

items.prompt: Correct the error — or submit with nothing flagged if the sentence is already right.
What does “The exhibits, which were sealed, remain confidential” tell the reader?
options: All of the exhibits were sealed
Only the sealed exhibits are confidential
items.explanation: A nonessential (comma) clause describes the whole group. Drop the commas and “which” becomes “that,” and now only some exhibits — the sealed ones — are covered. The punctuation changes the holding.

items.prompt: Which is correct?
options: The officers who responded first testified.
The officers which responded first testified.
The officers, that responded first, testified.
items.explanation: People take who. “Which” is for things and groups; “that” can take people but never follows a comma.

items.prompt: Correct the error — or submit with nothing flagged if the sentence is already right.
Why is “That which does not kill you makes you stronger” acceptable?
options: Writers use “which” to avoid a clumsy “that that”
items.explanation: The Blue Book's Rule 3: when “that” has already appeared, writers may use “which” for the next clause to avoid awkward doubling.

items.prompt: Correct the error — or submit with nothing flagged if the sentence is already right.

errors.explanation: “That” never follows a comma. The clause is essential — it says which affidavits — so delete the comma and keep “that.”

items.prompt: “My brother Daniel testified” vs. “My brother, Daniel, testified.” What changed?
options: The commas say Daniel is my only brother
The commas say Daniel is one of several brothers
items.explanation: No commas = essential = you need the name to know which brother, so there are others. Commas = nonessential = there is only one brother. The Blue Book's Mark Twain example makes the same point about book titles.

items.prompt: Which sentence says the company has exactly one subsidiary?
options: The company's subsidiary, Ardent Logistics, filed for bankruptcy.
The company's subsidiary Ardent Logistics filed for bankruptcy.
items.explanation: The commas make the name nonessential — droppable — which is only true if there is one subsidiary. In a bench memo, that difference is a fact about the record.

items.prompt: Correct the error — or submit with nothing flagged if the sentence is already right.

units.title: Adjectives and Adverbs
units.recap: Adjectives modify nouns; adverbs modify verbs, adjectives, and other adverbs. Sense and linking verbs (taste, smell, look, feel, seem) take adjectives — you feel bad, not badly. Good is the adjective; well is its adverb, and also an adjective about health. Use the comparative (-er/more) for two things and the superlative (-est/most) for three or more.

items.prompt: Correct the error — or submit with nothing flagged if the sentence is already right.

errors.explanation: Feel here is a linking verb describing her state, not an action performed with fingers — so it takes the adjective: felt bad.

items.prompt: Which is correct?
items.explanation: Sound is a linking verb here — it describes the argument, so an adjective follows. (An adverb would mean the argument is doing the sounding with skill.)

items.prompt: Which is correct?
options: The clerk did the job well.
The clerk did the job good.
items.explanation: Good is an adjective (a good job); well is its adverb (did it well). “Did good” means something else entirely — charitable work.

items.prompt: Correct the error — or submit with nothing flagged if the sentence is already right.

errors.explanation: The word describes how she answered — a verb — so it needs the adverb form: quickly.

items.prompt: Correct the error — or submit with nothing flagged if the sentence is already right.

errors.explanation: Two things take the comparative (more/-er); three or more take the superlative (most/-est). Of the two, the injunction is the more practical.

items.prompt: Which is correct?
options: Which of the three drafts reads best?
Which of the three drafts reads better?
items.explanation: Three or more → superlative. With only two, “better” would be right.

items.prompt: Correct the error — or submit with nothing flagged if the sentence is already right.

errors.explanation: In formal usage, don't drop the -ly when comparing adverbs: moved more quickly. (Same reason we write “talk more quietly,” not “talk quieter.”)

items.prompt: “The judge looked skeptically at counsel” vs. “The judge looked skeptical.” Are both correct?
options: Yes — the first describes how she looked at him; the second describes her appearance
No, only the first is correct
No, only the second is correct
items.explanation: When the eyes are actively doing the looking, use the adverb. When you are describing appearance or state, use the adjective. Same verb, two jobs.

items.prompt: Which reports that the witness has recovered from illness?
items.explanation: Well doubles as an adjective when it refers to health. “Looks good” is about appearance.

items.prompt: In “This holding controls,” what part of speech is “This”?
items.explanation: This, that, these, and those are adjectives when a noun follows them and pronouns when one doesn't (“This controls”).

items.prompt: Correct the error — or submit with nothing flagged if the sentence is already right.

errors.explanation: The word describes how counsel responded — an adverb job. “Respond” isn't a linking verb, so the adjective can't stand.

units.title: Prepositions
units.recap: Ending a sentence with a preposition is not an error — but dangling extra prepositions is (“Where is it at?”). Like means “similar to” and takes an object, not a clause; use as, as if, as though, or the way when a verb follows. “Of” is never a substitute for “have.” Prefer different from. Use into for motion, in for location.

items.prompt: Correct the error — or submit with nothing flagged if the sentence is already right.

errors.explanation: The extra preposition adds nothing: “where the exhibits were filed” is complete. Note this is different from the split-infinitive myth — dangling extras are a real fault.

items.prompt: Is “That is the statute the parties disagree about” acceptable?
options: Yes — ending with a preposition is not an error; recast only if it reads better
No — write “about which the parties disagree” always
No — it is always an error
items.explanation: The Blue Book calls the no-terminal-preposition rule an undying myth. Only delete prepositions that are genuinely surplus.

items.prompt: Correct the error — or submit with nothing flagged if the sentence is already right.

errors.explanation: A verb follows (“did”), so use as, as if, as though, or the way. Like means “similar to” and takes an object, not a clause.

items.prompt: Which is correct?
options: The dissent reads as if it were a majority opinion.
The dissent reads like it were a majority opinion.
items.explanation: Subject + verb follows, so “as if.” (Notice the subjunctive “were” as well — a contrary-to-fact statement.)

items.prompt: Which is correct?
options: The clerk, like most clerks, keeps a style sheet.
The clerk, as most clerks, keeps a style sheet.
items.explanation: No verb follows, so “like” (similar to) is right. Use “as” only when a verb is involved: as most clerks do.

items.prompt: Correct the error — or submit with nothing flagged if the sentence is already right.

errors.explanation: “Should of” is a mishearing of “should've.” The helping verb is have — never the preposition of.

items.prompt: Which does the Blue Book call unchallengeable?
options: This case is different from Sandoval.
This case is different than Sandoval.
items.explanation: “Different than” is not flatly incorrect, but it reads as sloppy to many literate readers. If “from” fits without a rewrite, use it.

items.prompt: Correct the error — or submit with nothing flagged if the sentence is already right.

errors.explanation: Use into for motion or inquiry (looked into the matter); in tells location (the file is in the drawer).

items.prompt: Which is correct?
options: Please get off of the podium.
items.explanation: “Off of” carries a surplus preposition. The same instinct fixes “outside of” and “inside of.”

items.prompt: In “We had never met before,” what is “before”?
options: An adverb — it has no object
items.explanation: A preposition isn't a preposition without a related noun or pronoun as its object. In “before noon,” it is; standing alone, it's an adverb.

units.title: Effective Writing
units.recap: Prefer concrete language and the active voice. Trim expletive openers (there is, it is) that bury the real subject. Avoid pointless double negatives. Keep listed ideas in the same grammatical form. An opening participial phrase must describe the subject that follows it, and modifiers belong next to what they modify.

items.prompt: Which is the strongest revision of “A decision was reached by the panel”?
options: It was decided by the panel.
items.explanation: Active voice puts the actor in front of the verb and cuts three words. (Passive still has legitimate uses — when the actor is unknown or beside the point.)

items.prompt: Which is the best revision of “There are three issues that must be resolved”?
options: There exist three issues to resolve.
It is three issues that must be resolved.
items.explanation: “There is/there are” openers push the real subject behind the verb and pad the sentence. Delete the expletive and the sentence stands up.

items.prompt: Which is the cleaner sentence?
options: The parties are willing to mediate.
The parties are not unwilling to mediate.
items.explanation: Two negatives making a positive is usually pompous. (Occasionally a “not un-” is genuinely apt — “uneven but not uninteresting” — but not by default.)

items.prompt: Correct the error — or submit with nothing flagged if the sentence is already right.

errors.explanation: Noun, noun, then an infinitive breaks the series. Make all three nouns: notice, disclosure, and preservation of the records.

items.prompt: Correct the error — or submit with nothing flagged if the sentence is already right.

errors.explanation: Errors cannot review a record. The opening participle must attach to the subject that follows — supply the actor: “we found several errors.”

items.prompt: Which version says the hearing — not the objection — happened on Friday?
options: On Friday, the court heard the objection filed last month.
The court heard the objection filed on Friday.
items.explanation: Trailing modifiers grab the nearest noun. Fronting the time phrase pins it to the hearing.

items.prompt: Correct the error — or submit with nothing flagged if the sentence is already right.

errors.explanation: A dependent clause standing alone is a fragment — it needs an independent clause to lean on. (Deliberate fragments are a stylistic choice; an orphaned “although” clause is just unfinished.)

items.prompt: Which is the more concrete sentence?
options: The county missed the filing deadline by nine days.
There were issues of a temporal nature with the county's submission.
items.explanation: Concrete beats vague: name the actor, the act, and the number. Vague phrasing raises questions the reader shouldn't have to ask.

items.prompt: When is the passive voice the better choice?
options: When the actor is unknown, obvious, or beside the point
Never — always use the active voice
Whenever the sentence would otherwise be short
items.explanation: “My watch was stolen” is the right sentence when you don't know the thief. The abuse to avoid is the responsibility-dodging “Mistakes were made.”

items.prompt: Correct the error — or submit with nothing flagged if the sentence is already right.

units.title: Grammar Mastery Test
units.recap: A mixed test across everything in Chapter 1 — agreement, pronouns, who/whom, adjectives and adverbs, prepositions, and effective writing. No warm-ups, no hints about which rule is being tested. That is exactly the condition you proofread in.

items.prompt: Correct the error — or submit with nothing flagged if the sentence is already right.

errors.explanation: Series is the singular subject; “of amended complaints” is just scenery.

items.prompt: Correct the error — or submit with nothing flagged if the sentence is already right.
Correct the error — or submit with nothing flagged if the sentence is already right.

errors.explanation: Two items → comparative. Between the two, the Ninth is the busier.

items.prompt: Correct the error — or submit with nothing flagged if the sentence is already right.

errors.explanation: Strip the compound: myself reviewed the petition? No. Use I — and reserve “myself” for sentences where I or me already appears.

items.prompt: Correct the error — or submit with nothing flagged if the sentence is already right.

errors.explanation: Contrary to fact — I am not in her position — so the subjunctive “were.”

items.prompt: Correct the error — or submit with nothing flagged if the sentence is already right.

errors.explanation: Essential clause identifying which arguments → “that,” no comma.

items.prompt: Correct the error — or submit with nothing flagged if the sentence is already right.

errors.explanation: The argument didn't fail to object — a party did. The participial opener must describe the subject that follows.

items.prompt: Correct the error — or submit with nothing flagged if the sentence is already right.

errors.explanation: Draw → drew → drawn. After “had,” use the participle.

items.prompt: Correct the error — or submit with nothing flagged if the sentence is already right.
Correct the error — or submit with nothing flagged if the sentence is already right.

errors.explanation: A subject and verb follow, so use “as” (or “the way”). Reserve “like” for comparisons with a plain object.

items.prompt: Correct the error — or submit with nothing flagged if the sentence is already right.

errors.explanation: “It is clear” → It's. The second “its” is a correct possessive — the sentence needs both forms, one word apart.

items.prompt: Correct the error — or submit with nothing flagged if the sentence is already right.

errors.explanation: Portion words take their number from the noun after “of” — commissioners, plural.

items.prompt: Correct the error — or submit with nothing flagged if the sentence is already right.

errors.explanation: Objects of a preposition take the object form: between the county and us taxpayers.

items.prompt: Correct the error — or submit with nothing flagged if the sentence is already right.

errors.explanation: Never pair the contraction “there's” with a plural subject. Better still, cut the expletive: “Several reasons support affirmance.”

items.prompt: Correct the error — or submit with nothing flagged if the sentence is already right.
